headline: High: OpenHands’ broad runtime/tool access can amplify ms-swift outputs into unsafe actions, while shared file-based workflows create leakage and conflict risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ms-swift reads/writes files and uses stdin/stdout plus CLI/Python workflows, while OpenHands can use MCP, browser, shell, and editor actions inside a runtime. If OpenHands ingests ms-swift-generated text from shared files or prompts, instruction-like content could steer tool use. The shared bridge is plausible, but not proven by direct pair evidence.
conditions: IF OpenHands reads ms-swift output from a shared file or prompt, injection becomes plausible.
IF either agent treats file content as instructions without provenance checks, the risk materializes.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Require provenance tags on any ms-swift output before OpenHands consumes it.
Disable automatic prompt ingestion from files.
Review tool-call prompts for instruction-like content before execution.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ms-swift handles hub_token and sdk-token and touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration data; OpenHands handles model provider API keys and files in its runtime sandbox. Because OpenHands has broad network egress and file access, a shared workspace or mounted volume could expose sensitive artifacts from ms-swift to OpenHands outputs or external APIs. The exact sharing mechanism is not stated, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same mounted files, leakage risk exists.
IF OpenHands forwards ms-swift artifacts to a model provider, secrets may leave the boundary.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared directories.
Mount only least-privilege files into OpenHands.
Redact tokens from ms-swift logs before handoff.
Block outbound access for runs that process sensitive artifacts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, install packages, read/write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses. OpenHands also modifies git state and supports multiple instances via mounted volume, while ms-swift writes files and has no stated isolation. On a shared directory or repo, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide and corrupt state; the lack of explicit locking makes the default pair unsafe enough to rate high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory, write conflicts are possible.
IF OpenHands instances share a mounted volume, concurrent mutation can corrupt files or git state.
mitigations: Use separate working directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Disable git writes in OpenHands for shared repos.
Run only one agent per mounted volume.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ms-swift can emit training, evaluation, and configuration outputs, and OpenHands is an action-taking coding agent with shell, browser, and editor tools. If OpenHands treats ms-swift output as authoritative, it may commit, edit, or execute based on unverified content. That creates a direct cascade from generated text to real actions, with no built-in verification shown in either profile.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses ms-swift output as task instructions or code without verification, cascading errors occur.
IF ms-swift produces incorrect facts or configs, OpenHands can operationalize them into actions.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Add a verification step for all ms-swift outputs.
Restrict OpenHands to read-only analysis mode for handoffs.
Use schema validation on generated artifacts.

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token, sdk-token, and multiple sensitive data classes, while OpenHands handles model provider API keys and runs in a Docker runtime with broad egress. The pair can therefore move sensitive data between environments with different retention and residency assumptions, but the profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction or regulated data class like PHI. That makes this a compliance-mismatch risk, not a residency breach claim.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either runtime, retention and logging policies must align.
IF OpenHands forwards sensitive artifacts to external model providers, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Document data-handling boundaries.
Disable retention of sensitive logs.
Keep regulated data out of both runtimes.
Review provider terms before enabling external calls.
